q: If we sell fertiliser, do farm N2O emissions go in our Scope 3 Category 11?
title: Fertiliser sellers and Category 11 N2O
short: Yes. Nitrogen fertiliser forms nitrous oxide in the soil when it is used, so a maker or distributor reports those emissions in Scope 3 Category 11, use of sold products, for the tonnes sold in the year. Urea sellers also report the CO2 from the carbon in urea.
audience: Fertiliser makers, agri input distributors and agritech platforms

sections.h: Why it counts as a direct use-phase emission
p: The GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard requires direct use-phase emissions in Category 11. These include products that contain or form greenhouse gases released during use. Nitrogen fertiliser fits that description: the N2O forms from the product's own nitrogen once it is in the soil, not from energy the farmer uses.

ul: Direct N2O: kg N sold x 0.01 kg N2O-N per kg N (IPCC 2006 default).
Indirect N2O from volatilisation (10% of synthetic N, then 0.01) and leaching (30% of N, then 0.0075). Include them or say you left them out.
Urea CO2: 0.733 t CO2 per tonne of urea.
Convert N2O-N to N2O with 44/28 and name the GWP, for example 273 (IPCC AR6).

sections.h: Who else reports the same emissions
p: The farmer reports them in Scope 1. A maker and its distributors each report them in Category 11 for the volume they sell. That overlap is expected in Scope 3; it is not double counting within one company's inventory.

sections.h: Keep it apart from your own footprint
p: Emissions from making ammonia and urea at your plant are your Scope 1 and 2. Purchased fertiliser you resell carries upstream emissions in Category 1. Use-phase N2O sits only in Category 11. Report all lifetime emissions in the year of sale.
